name: Patek Philippe
tagline: Geneva's family-owned benchmark for grand complications since 1839
summary: Patek Philippe is widely regarded as the most prestigious watch manufacturer in the world, famed for its grand complications, perpetual calendars and the Nautilus. Owned by the Stern family since 1932, it remains one of the last independent, family-run Genevan manufactures and dominates the high end of the auction market.
history:
Patek Philippe traces its origins to 1839, when Polish émigrés Antoni Patek and Franciszek Czapek founded Patek, Czapek & Co. in Geneva. After the partners split in 1844, Patek teamed up with French watchmaker Jean Adrien Philippe, inventor of a keyless winding and hand-setting system, and in 1851 the firm became Patek Philippe & Co. Royal clients followed quickly: Queen Victoria acquired a Patek pendant watch at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London.

The firm built its reputation on precision and complications. It made what is considered the first Swiss wristwatch in 1868 for the Hungarian Countess Koscowicz, the first perpetual-calendar wristwatch in 1925, and in 1933 delivered the Henry Graves Jr. Supercomplication, a pocket watch with 24 complications that sold for more than CHF 23 million in 2014.

The Great Depression brought the company to the brink, and in 1932 it was bought by Charles and Jean Stern, owners of a dial-making firm. The Stern family has controlled it ever since, passing leadership from Henri Stern to Philippe Stern and, in 2009, to Thierry Stern. The brand weathered the quartz crisis by staying resolutely mechanical and, in 1976, launched Gérald Genta's steel Nautilus, which would later become one of the most sought-after watches in the world. The 1989 Calibre 89, with 33 complications, marked the company's 150th anniversary.

In 1996 Patek consolidated production at a large manufacture in Plan-les-Ouates outside Geneva, and in 2009 it replaced the Geneva Seal with its own stricter Patek Philippe Seal. Today it produces an estimated 70,000 watches a year, discontinued the fabled Nautilus 5711 in 2021, launched the Cubitus in 2024, and still consistently holds the record for the most expensive wristwatches ever sold at auction.

name: Audemars Piguet
tagline: The Le Brassus family manufacture that invented the luxury steel sports watch
summary: Audemars Piguet is the oldest fine watch manufacture still in the hands of its founding families, based in Le Brassus in the Vallée de Joux. Its 1972 Royal Oak created the luxury steel sports-watch category, and the brand remains one of the 'Holy Trinity' of Swiss watchmaking alongside Patek Philippe and Vacheron Constantin.
history:
Audemars Piguet was founded in 1875 in Le Brassus, in the Vallée de Joux, by two young watchmakers, Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet. Audemars handled the technical side while Piguet ran sales, and the firm was formally registered as Audemars Piguet & Cie in 1881. From the start it specialised in complicated movements, producing grand complication pocket watches and, in 1892, a minute repeater movement small enough for a wristwatch.

The Great Depression and the Second World War slashed production, but the company survived by focusing on ultra-thin and complicated pieces, including the 1946 ultra-thin calibre 2003, then the world's thinnest. By the early 1970s, with the quartz crisis threatening mechanical watchmaking, managing director Georges Golay commissioned Gérald Genta to design a radically new watch. The result, the 1972 Royal Oak ref. 5402ST, was an octagonal-bezelled steel sports watch with an integrated bracelet priced above many gold watches. It was controversial at first but ultimately defined an entire category.

The Royal Oak Offshore followed in 1993, an oversized and aggressive variant nicknamed 'the Beast', and in 1986 AP released the first automatic tourbillon wristwatch. Under CEO François-Henry Bennahmias (2012–2023) the company cut back its wholesale network, pushed into directly operated boutiques and 'AP Houses', and saw revenues soar. The Code 11.59 collection was launched in 2019, and the Musée Atelier Audemars Piguet, a spiralling glass building by BIG, opened in Le Brassus in 2020.

The company is still owned by descendants of the Audemars and Piguet families. Ilaria Resta became CEO in 2024, and for its 150th anniversary in 2025 AP unveiled the Universelle RD#4, its most complicated watch to date with more than 40 functions.

name: Vacheron Constantin
tagline: The oldest watch manufacture in continuous operation, Geneva since 1755
summary: Founded in Geneva in 1755, Vacheron Constantin claims more than 270 years of uninterrupted production, making it the oldest continuously operating watch manufacture in the world. Part of Richemont since 1996, it is the third member of the 'Holy Trinity' and is renowned for grand complications, métiers d'art and the Overseas sports watch.
history:
Vacheron Constantin began in 1755 when 24-year-old Jean-Marc Vacheron, a master watchmaker in Geneva, took on his first apprentice, a contract that survives as the brand's birth certificate. His descendants expanded the business, and in 1819 Jacques-Barthélemy Vacheron went into partnership with the merchant François Constantin, who travelled Europe selling the firm's watches under the motto 'do better if possible, and that is always possible'.

In 1839 the company hired Georges-Auguste Leschot, whose pantograph and machine tools allowed standardised, interchangeable movement parts, an industrial breakthrough for Swiss watchmaking. The Maltese cross, derived from a component of the going barrel, was registered as the brand's emblem in 1880. Vacheron Constantin became a supplier to royalty and the wealthy, producing ornate pocket watches for King Fuad I of Egypt and the American collector James Ward Packard.

The twentieth century brought turbulence. The Depression and the quartz crisis weakened the company, which passed through the hands of the Ketterer family and, in the 1990s, Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani, before being acquired by the Vendôme group, now Richemont, in 1996. Its 1977 ref. 222, an integrated-bracelet steel sports watch, paved the way for the Overseas, launched in 1996.

Under Richemont the manufacture moved to a modern headquarters in Plan-les-Ouates (2004) and returned to extreme complication. The Ref. 57260 pocket watch of 2015 featured 57 complications, the Les Cabinotiers Solaria of 2024 set a record for a wristwatch, and for its 270th anniversary in 2025 the house unveiled the Berkley Grand Complication with 63 complications. Its bespoke Les Cabinotiers department continues to create one-of-a-kind pieces for private clients.

name: Breguet
tagline: Abraham-Louis Breguet's legacy: the tourbillon, Breguet hands and guilloché
summary: Founded in Paris in 1775 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, perhaps the most influential watchmaker in history, Breguet invented the tourbillon and the first wristwatch. Now owned by the Swatch Group and based in the Vallée de Joux, it is known for engine-turned guilloché dials, blued 'pomme' hands and classical complications.
history:
Abraham-Louis Breguet, born in Neuchâtel in 1747, trained in France and opened his workshop on the Quai de l'Horloge in Paris in 1775. His innovations reshaped horology: the 'perpétuelle' self-winding watch of around 1780, the Breguet overcoil hairspring, the pare-chute shock protection of 1790, the ruby-cylinder escapement, the gong-spring for repeaters and, most famously, the tourbillon, patented in 1801 to counter the effects of gravity on the balance. He also designed the distinctive hands, numerals and engine-turned dials that still bear his name.

His clients included Marie-Antoinette, whose commissioned grand complication, No. 160, took more than four decades to finish, as well as Napoleon Bonaparte, the Duke of Wellington and Tsar Alexander I. In 1810 he began what is regarded as the first wristwatch, made for Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples. After Breguet's death in 1823 his son and grandson ran the company until 1870, when it passed to the English Brown family, who kept it for a century.

The twentieth century brought military chronographs for the French Air Force, notably the Type 20 from the 1950s, and a succession of owners: the Chaumet brothers in 1970, the investment group Investcorp in 1987 and, in 1999, the Swatch Group under Nicolas G. Hayek, who revived the manufacture at L'Abbaye in the Vallée de Joux and commissioned a replica of the lost Marie-Antoinette watch, completed in 2008.

Today Breguet produces the Classique, Tradition, Marine, Type XX and Reine de Naples collections, combining in-house guilloché and complications. In 2025 the brand celebrated its 250th anniversary with a series of commemorative models and new technical developments.

name: Jaeger-LeCoultre
tagline: The 'watchmaker's watchmaker' of the Vallée de Joux, home of the Reverso
summary: Jaeger-LeCoultre is a highly vertically integrated manufacture in Le Sentier that has created more than 1,200 calibres and historically supplied movements to Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin. Owned by Richemont, it is famous for the swivelling Reverso, the Atmos clock and technically ambitious complications.
history:
In 1833 the self-taught watchmaker Antoine LeCoultre opened a small workshop in Le Sentier in the Vallée de Joux to make precision gear-wheel components. In 1844 he invented the Millionomètre, the first instrument able to measure to a micron, and in 1847 a keyless winding and time-setting system that did away with the key. By 1866 LeCoultre & Cie had become the valley's first manufacture to bring all watchmaking crafts under one roof, earning its reputation as the 'Grande Maison'.

Around 1903 the Paris-based naval chronometer maker Edmond Jaeger challenged Swiss manufacturers to produce his ultra-thin movements, and Jacques-David LeCoultre took up the challenge. The collaboration produced the record-thin calibre 145 pocket watch in 1907 and, in 1929, the Calibre 101, still the world's smallest mechanical movement. The Atmos clock, which draws its energy from small changes in temperature, followed in 1928, and in 1931 the Reverso, a rectangular watch whose case flips over to protect the crystal from polo mallets. The two families formally merged under the Jaeger-LeCoultre name in 1937.

Mid-century hits included the Memovox alarm watch and the anti-magnetic Geophysic chronometer of 1958. After difficult quartz-era years, the company came under VDO (1978) and Mannesmann before being acquired by Richemont in 2000. The Master Control line of 1992 introduced the '1000 Hours Control' test, and the Gyrotourbillon (2004), Duomètre dual-wing movements (2007) and the Hybris Mechanica grand complications reasserted its technical ambitions.

Today Jaeger-LeCoultre remains the largest employer in the Vallée de Joux, producing most components in-house across roughly 180 crafts, while the Reverso, Master and Polaris lines anchor its collection.

name: Blancpain
tagline: Claimed oldest watch brand and creator of the Fifty Fathoms dive watch
summary: Blancpain traces its roots to 1735 in Villeret, making it one of the oldest watch brands in existence. Revived in the 1980s and owned by the Swatch Group since 1992, it is best known for the 1953 Fifty Fathoms, the archetype of the modern diver's watch, and for traditional complications such as the full calendar with moon phase.
history:
Blancpain dates its founding to 1735, when schoolteacher and watchmaker Jehan-Jacques Blancpain registered as a watchmaker in Villeret, in the Bernese Jura. For almost two centuries the business passed from father to son, industrialising under Frédéric-Louis Blancpain in the 19th century. When the family line ended in 1932, the company was taken over by Betty Fiechter and André Léal and renamed Rayville SA, although Blancpain remained the brand name. It supplied movements for the Harwood automatic wristwatch of 1926 and produced the Rolls automatic in 1930.

In 1953, CEO Jean-Jacques Fiechter, a keen diver, developed the Fifty Fathoms, a robust automatic watch with a locking rotating bezel, luminous markers and a sealed case. It was adopted by the French Navy's combat swimmers under Captain Robert Maloubier and later worn in Jacques-Yves Cousteau's documentary The Silent World. Blancpain joined the SSIH group (Omega and Tissot) in 1961, but the quartz crisis devastated the business and production effectively stopped by the early 1980s.

In 1983 Jean-Claude Biver and Jacques Piguet bought the dormant name and relaunched it in Le Brassus with the famous slogan that Blancpain had never made a quartz watch and never would. They focused on six 'masterpieces' of traditional watchmaking, culminating in the 1991 '1735' grand complication. The success attracted SMH, the future Swatch Group, which acquired the brand in 1992.

Under Marc A. Hayek, president from 2002, Blancpain relaunched the Fifty Fathoms in 2003, developed in-house calibres including the carrousel and the Villeret collection's complete calendars, and supported ocean exploration through its Ocean Commitment programme. The Fifty Fathoms celebrated its 70th anniversary in 2023.

name: Piaget
tagline: Ultra-thin movement specialist and master of gold, gems and colour
summary: Piaget grew from a 19th-century movement workshop in the Jura into a Richemont-owned maison famous for ultra-thin watchmaking and jewellery watches. Its Altiplano holds multiple thinness records, while the Piaget Polo is one of the original luxury integrated-bracelet designs.
history:
In 1874 Georges Édouard Piaget set up a workshop in his family farmhouse in La Côte-aux-Fées, in the Swiss Jura, making high-precision movements and components for other brands. For decades the company worked anonymously as a supplier until his grandsons Gérald and Valentin Piaget registered the Piaget name in 1943 and began selling complete watches under their own brand.

The post-war years established the house's two pillars. In 1957 Valentin Piaget developed the calibre 9P, a hand-wound movement just 2 mm thick, and in 1960 the 12P, then the world's thinnest self-winding movement at 2.3 mm, which earned a place in the Guinness Book of Records. The thin movements freed space for creativity, and from 1964 Piaget pioneered hard-stone dials in lapis lazuli, turquoise, onyx and tiger's eye. In 1959 it opened a Geneva workshop for gold-setting and jewellery, and its bold gold cuff watches became emblems of 1960s and 70s glamour worn by Andy Warhol and Hollywood stars.

In 1979 Yves Piaget launched the Piaget Polo, an all-gold watch whose horizontal gadroons flowed seamlessly from case to bracelet, and it became a symbol of 1980s luxury. The family sold the company to the Vendôme group, now Richemont, in 1988, although Yves Piaget remained an ambassador. Manufacturing is split between La Côte-aux-Fées for movements and Plan-les-Ouates near Geneva for cases, jewellery and assembly.

In the 21st century Piaget returned to record-breaking: the Altiplano Ultimate Concept became the world's thinnest mechanical watch at 2 mm in 2018 and entered series production in 2020. The Polo was relaunched as a steel sports watch in 2016 and again in 2021, and the house celebrated its 150th anniversary in 2024 with a re-edition of the Polo 79.

name: Chopard
tagline: Scheufele family jeweller-watchmaker behind Happy Diamonds and L.U.C
summary: Chopard is a family-owned Geneva maison that combines high jewellery with serious watchmaking through its Fleurier-based L.U.C manufacture. Owned by the Scheufele family since 1963, it is known for the floating diamonds of Happy Sport, the Alpine Eagle sports watch, and its long partnerships with the Cannes Film Festival and the Mille Miglia.
history:
Louis-Ulysse Chopard founded his workshop in 1860 in Sonvilier, in the Bernese Jura, making precise pocket watches and chronometers that found customers across Europe and Russia. His son Paul-Louis moved the company to Geneva in 1937, but by the early 1960s the family had no successor willing to take over.

In 1963 the business was bought by Karl Scheufele III, heir to a Pforzheim jewellery and watchmaking family. Under Karl and his wife Karin, Chopard grew into an international jeweller-watchmaker, building a manufacture in Meyrin-Geneva in 1974. Designer Ronald Kurowski's Happy Diamonds of 1976, with loose diamonds dancing between two sapphire crystals, became a signature, and in 1993 Happy Sport became one of the first watches to combine steel and diamonds. The 1980 St. Moritz, Karl-Friedrich Scheufele's first design, introduced a steel sports watch with integrated bracelet.

Karl-Friedrich Scheufele, a passionate car enthusiast, linked the brand to the Mille Miglia race in 1988 and in 1996 founded Chopard Manufacture in Fleurier to produce high-end movements. The first in-house calibre, the micro-rotor L.U.C 96.01-L, appeared in 1997 and was named after the founder. His sister Caroline Scheufele took charge of jewellery and, from 1998, the redesign of the Cannes Film Festival's Palme d'Or, which Chopard has crafted ever since.

Today Karl-Friedrich and Caroline are co-presidents. In 2019 the Alpine Eagle revived the St. Moritz with Lucent Steel, and since 2018 Chopard has committed to using 100% ethically sourced gold. L.U.C Fleurier Quality Foundation certification and in-house tourbillons, chiming watches and perpetual calendars have given the brand genuine haute horlogerie credibility.

name: Girard-Perregaux
tagline: Home of the Three Gold Bridges tourbillon and the octagonal Laureato
summary: Girard-Perregaux is a La Chaux-de-Fonds manufacture tracing its lineage to 1791, celebrated for the Tourbillon with Three Gold Bridges and the 1975 Laureato. After years under Kering, it was bought by its management in 2022 and is run alongside Ulysse Nardin within the Sowind Group.
history:
Girard-Perregaux dates its origins to 1791, when Jean-François Bautte, a Geneva watchmaker and jeweller, began signing his own timepieces. The modern name was born in 1856 after watchmaker Constant Girard married Marie Perregaux, daughter of a Le Locle watchmaking family, and set up Girard-Perregaux in La Chaux-de-Fonds. In 1906 the firm absorbed the Bautte business, uniting the two lineages.

Constant Girard's masterpiece was the Tourbillon with Three Gold Bridges, a pocket watch whose movement architecture reduced the bridges to three parallel gold arrows; it won a gold medal at the 1889 Paris Universal Exhibition and remains the house's emblem. Around 1880 the company produced early series wristwatches for officers of the German Imperial Navy, among the first wristwatches made in quantity.

In the 20th century the brand was an innovator in precision: the Gyromatic HF of 1966 was an early high-frequency automatic, and in 1970 Girard-Perregaux introduced a quartz movement running at 32,768 Hz, the frequency still used by almost all quartz watches. The Laureato, an octagonal-bezelled steel sports watch with integrated bracelet, followed in 1975.

The quartz crisis and changing ownership brought difficult years until Italian architect and racing driver Luigi Macaluso took control in 1992, restoring in-house manufacturing and launching the Sowind Group. The French group PPR, later Kering, acquired a majority stake from 2008 and full control in 2011, but in 2022 Kering sold Sowind, including Ulysse Nardin, to a management team led by Patrick Pruniaux. The Laureato was relaunched in 2016 and remains the brand's bestseller, alongside Bridges and the dressy 1966 collection.

name: Ulysse Nardin
tagline: Le Locle's marine-chronometer maker turned pioneer of silicon and the Freak
summary: Founded in Le Locle in 1846, Ulysse Nardin built its fame on marine chronometers used by dozens of navies. Revived in the 1980s with astronomical watches and the radical Freak, it pioneered silicon components and is now independent alongside Girard-Perregaux in the Sowind Group.
history:
Ulysse Nardin founded his company in Le Locle in 1846, specialising in precision pocket watches and, above all, marine chronometers. His son Paul-David Nardin expanded the business, and the firm's chronometers won thousands of awards at observatory competitions and international exhibitions. At one point Ulysse Nardin marine chronometers equipped around 50 of the world's navies, and the anchor became the brand's emblem.

The quartz crisis nearly finished the company, and by 1983 it was on the verge of disappearing when Swiss entrepreneur Rolf Schnyder bought it. Schnyder partnered with the watchmaker and scholar Ludwig Oechslin, who designed the 'Trilogy of Time': the Astrolabium Galileo Galilei of 1985, the Planetarium Copernicus of 1988 and the Tellurium Johannes Kepler of 1992. Oechslin's 1996 GMT± Perpetual introduced a perpetual calendar adjustable forwards and backwards with the crown.

In 2001 Ulysse Nardin launched the Freak, a watch without dial, hands or crown in which the entire movement rotates to show the time. It used silicon for escapement components, a material the company then developed through its affiliate Sigatec, making it a pioneer of silicon technology now used across the industry. The brand also launched the Maxi Marine and Diver collections, rooted in its nautical heritage.

After Schnyder's death in 2011, the French group Kering acquired Ulysse Nardin in 2014 and later placed it alongside Girard-Perregaux in the Sowind Group. In 2022 Kering sold both brands to their management under Patrick Pruniaux. Today the brand's collections are the Freak, Diver, Marine and the angular Blast, positioning it as a technically daring independent.

name: Parmigiani Fleurier
tagline: A master restorer's manufacture in Fleurier, backed by the Sandoz Family Foundation
summary: Parmigiani Fleurier was founded in 1996 by master restorer Michel Parmigiani with the backing of the Sandoz Family Foundation. Vertically integrated through its sister companies, including movement maker Vaucher, it is known for refined, understated watches such as the Tonda PF with its knurled bezel.
history:
Michel Parmigiani, born in 1950, trained as a watchmaker in Fleurier and in 1976 opened his own workshop, Parmigiani Mesure et Art du Temps, specialising in the restoration of antique clocks, automata and complicated pocket watches. His skill brought him to the attention of the Sandoz Family Foundation, the charitable holding of the pharmaceutical family, for whom he restored its important collection of historic timepieces.

In 1996 the foundation acquired a majority of his business and launched Parmigiani Fleurier as a watch brand, debuting with the Toric collection, whose knurled bezel recalled classical architectural ornament. The Kalpa tonneau followed in 1998. Over the next decade the foundation built a remarkable network of suppliers in the Val-de-Travers: Vaucher Manufacture Fleurier for movements, Les Artisans Boîtiers for cases, Quadrance et Habillage for dials and Atokalpa for components. Vaucher also supplies movements to other brands, and Hermès took a stake in it in 2006.

Parmigiani became known for exceptional finishing, for bespoke pieces and for a long partnership with Bugatti that produced the Bugatti Type 370 in 2004, with its transverse, engine-like movement. It also restored and built unique objects, from pocket watches to clocks.

In 2019 Guido Terreni, previously of Bulgari, became CEO and refocused the brand around quiet luxury. The Tonda PF, launched in 2021 with an integrated bracelet, platinum knurled bezel and barleycorn guilloché dial, became the brand's breakthrough success. The Tonda PF Minute Rattrapante and the relaunched Toric followed, and Parmigiani remains owned by the Sandoz Family Foundation.

name: Roger Dubuis
tagline: Geneva hyper-watches: skeletonised star bridges and Lamborghini links
summary: Roger Dubuis is a Geneva-based Richemont maison founded in 1995, known for flamboyant skeletonised watches with star-shaped bridges and long-standing adherence to the Geneva Seal. Its Excalibur and Knights of the Round Table collections, plus a partnership with Lamborghini Squadra Corse, define its 'hyper horology' positioning.
history:
Roger Dubuis was founded in Geneva in 1995 by watchmaker Roger Dubuis, who had spent years in the complications workshop of Patek Philippe, and the entrepreneur Carlos Dias. Its first collections, Hommage and Sympathie, were classical in design, but the company quickly distinguished itself by committing to have its movements certified with the Geneva Seal, the Poinçon de Genève, and by building its own manufacture in Meyrin.

In the 2000s the brand developed a bolder identity. The Excalibur, with its fluted bezel and triple lugs, became the flagship, and the Easy Diver and Golden Square added sportier and more exuberant shapes. The company produced large numbers of in-house calibres, including tourbillons and skeleton movements, in a remarkably short time.

Richemont took a 60% stake in 2008 and later full control, and after the founder stepped back the brand pivoted to what it calls 'hyper horology'. The star-shaped skeleton bridge became its signature, most notably in the Excalibur Double Flying Tourbillon and the Spider series. The Knights of the Round Table collection turned Arthurian figures into miniature sculptures around the dial. In 2017 Roger Dubuis partnered with Lamborghini Squadra Corse and Pirelli, launching Excalibur models with motorsport materials, rubber straps made from tyre compounds and the high-energy Monovortex and Duotor mechanisms.

Roger Dubuis himself died in 2017. Under Richemont the brand continues to produce limited, highly technical watches, typically in carbon, titanium, ceramic and composite cases, positioned firmly at the top end of the market.

name: Richard Mille
tagline: Racing machines on the wrist: ultra-light tonneau hyper-watches since 2001
summary: Richard Mille launched in 2001 and in two decades became one of the most valuable watch brands in the world, with an estimated CHF 1.75 billion in revenue from only about 6,000 watches a year. Its technical, tonneau-shaped watches in carbon TPT, titanium and ceramic are worn by elite athletes such as Rafael Nadal.
history:
Richard Mille, a French executive who had worked in watch and jewellery marketing at Matra and Mauboussin, set out in the late 1990s to build a watch using the materials and engineering logic of Formula 1 and aerospace. He partnered with Dominique Guenat, whose family business Horométrie in Les Breuleux in the Jura would manufacture the watches, and with the movement specialist Audemars Piguet Renaud & Papi. The first model, the RM 001 tourbillon, was presented in 2001 at a price that astonished the industry.

The brand's principle was that watches should be as comfortable and resistant as sports equipment. Its tonneau cases, skeletonised movements with titanium baseplates and innovative materials such as Carbon TPT and Quartz TPT made a distinctive visual language. Racing driver Felipe Massa wore the RM 011 flyback chronograph, launched in 2007, and in 2010 Rafael Nadal began competing with the RM 027 tourbillon, which weighed under 20 grams. Nadal won major titles wearing the watches, turning the brand into a global phenomenon.

Richard Mille remains independent and family controlled, with the Mille and Guenat families holding the business, and the founder's children now in senior roles. Production is deliberately limited to around 6,000 pieces a year, yet according to Morgan Stanley estimates the brand ranked sixth in the Swiss industry in 2025. Recent records include the RM UP-01 Ferrari of 2022, at 1.75 mm the thinnest mechanical watch at its launch, and the RM 27-05 for Nadal. Ambassadors range from Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc to sprinters and golfers, and a women's collection has grown around the RM 07-01.

name: Hublot
tagline: The 'Art of Fusion': gold meets rubber, ceramic meets sapphire
summary: Hublot, founded in 1980 by Carlo Crocco, shocked the industry by pairing a gold watch with a natural rubber strap. Reinvented by Jean-Claude Biver with the 2005 Big Bang and owned by LVMH since 2008, it is known for bold materials, sports sponsorships and the in-house Unico chronograph.
history:
Hublot was founded in 1980 by Carlo Crocco, an Italian from the Binda watch dynasty, under the company name MDM Genève. His first watch, with a porthole-shaped case (hublot means porthole in French) and a gold case on a natural rubber strap, was so unconventional that it was rejected by the Basel fair, yet it quickly found clients among European royalty. Developing a rubber strap that did not crack or smell took years of research.

By the early 2000s the brand had stagnated. In 2004 Jean-Claude Biver, who had revived Blancpain and led Omega's marketing, became CEO and shareholder. In 2005 he launched the Big Bang, a 44 mm chronograph combining steel, ceramic, rubber and Kevlar under the 'Art of Fusion' slogan. It won a design prize in Geneva and transformed Hublot's fortunes, with sales rising several-fold within a few years.

LVMH acquired Hublot in 2008. The brand built a manufacture in Nyon, launched the in-house Unico flyback chronograph in 2010 and developed proprietary materials such as Magic Gold, a scratch-resistant ceramic-gold alloy, and coloured sapphire cases. Sponsorships of football, including FIFA World Cup timekeeping, and ambassadors such as Usain Bolt and Pelé made it one of the most visible luxury brands. Ricardo Guadalupe succeeded Biver as CEO in 2012.

Today Hublot's collections include the Big Bang, Classic Fusion, Spirit of Big Bang, Square Bang and the high-end MP series, while the 2025 twentieth anniversary of the Big Bang celebrated its defining model.

name: Franck Muller

summary: Franck Muller was founded in 1991 by watchmaker Franck Muller and entrepreneur Vartan Sirmakes, and grew rapidly on the strength of complicated movements and the curvaceous Cintrée Curvex tonneau case. Based at its Watchland campus in Genthod near Geneva, it is known for the Crazy Hours, Vanguard and Casablanca.
history:
Franck Muller, born in 1958 to a Swiss father and Italian mother, studied at the Geneva watchmaking school and worked restoring antique pieces for collectors and auction houses. In the late 1980s he built a series of highly complicated wristwatches under his own name, including tourbillons and a perpetual calendar with minute repeater, earning a reputation as a prodigy.

In 1991 he joined forces with Vartan Sirmakes, a case maker of Armenian origin, to found the Franck Muller company. The brand quickly defined its identity with the Cintrée Curvex, a tonneau case curved in three dimensions, and exuberant dials with stylised Arabic numerals. The company built its headquarters, Watchland, a château-style campus at Genthod on the shores of Lake Geneva, and rapidly expanded into a group that included several smaller brands and component suppliers.

Throughout the 1990s and 2000s Franck Muller was among the fastest-growing Swiss brands, famous for the Master Banker with three time zones, the Long Island rectangular watch, the Conquistador sports line and, in 2003, the Crazy Hours, whose hour hand jumps between numerals placed out of order. In 2009 the Aeternitas Mega 4 was presented as the most complicated wristwatch in the world, with 36 complications.

The founders fell out publicly in the 2000s, and Sirmakes has since run the group. The Vanguard, a sportier Curvex design introduced in the 2010s, became a bestseller, and the brand remains privately owned, with a strong following in the Middle East and Asia.

name: Bovet
tagline: Fleurier's enamel-and-engraving specialist, once the watch of imperial China
summary: Bovet was founded in 1822 by Édouard Bovet, whose ornate pocket watches became so popular in China that the name became a byword for 'watch'. Owned since 2001 by Pascal Raffy, the independent house is known for hand engraving, miniature painting, the convertible Amadeo case and complicated Récital pieces.
history:
In 1814 Édouard Bovet, a young watchmaker from Fleurier in the Val-de-Travers, travelled to London and from there to Canton, the only Chinese port open to foreign trade. He sold four watches for the then enormous sum of 10,000 dollars and, recognising the Chinese appetite for richly decorated timepieces, founded Bovet with his brothers in 1822, with a workshop in Fleurier and a sales office in Canton. Their pocket watches, typically made in pairs and decorated with enamel miniatures, pearls and hand engraving, with fine movements visible through the back, became so desirable that 'Bo Wei' came to mean 'watch' in Chinese.

The firm prospered for much of the 19th century but declined as the China trade waned, passing through several owners over the following century. In 2001 the Swiss entrepreneur and collector Pascal Raffy bought the company and set about restoring its standing as a fully fledged manufacture. In 2006 he acquired the Dimier 1738 manufacture, giving Bovet its own movement and component production, including hairsprings, and he established the brand's base in Fleurier with a workshop at the Château de Môtiers.

Under Raffy, Bovet developed the patented Amadeo convertible case, which lets a single watch be worn as a wristwatch, a pocket watch, a pendant or a table clock. The house became known for extremely decorated métiers d'art pieces and for complications such as the Récital 20 Astérium astronomical watch and the Récital 22 Grand Récital. Bovet remains fully independent and produces only a small number of watches each year, many as bespoke pieces through its Ateliers Bovet programme.

history:
Jacob Arabo, born in Uzbekistan and raised in Queens after his family emigrated to the United States, trained as a jeweller and opened his own business in New York's Diamond District in 1986. His bold, colourful designs and personal relationships with musicians made 'Jacob the Jeweler' a household name in hip-hop culture during the 1990s, and his work was name-checked in numerous songs.

In 2002 he launched the Five Time Zone watch, a colourful quartz watch with four subdials that became a celebrity hit and moved the brand into watches. Arabo then pushed into high horology, setting up Jacob & Co. operations in Geneva and collaborating with specialist movement makers. The Astronomia, launched in 2014, features a vertical, multi-axis tourbillon, a rotating globe and a spherically cut diamond all orbiting the dial, and became the brand's signature.

The brand also created the Billionaire watch, set with hundreds of carats of emerald-cut diamonds, and a series of musical watches such as the Opera Godfather, which plays the film's theme. Partnerships with Bugatti produced the Bugatti Chiron Tourbillon, whose miniature W16 engine animates at the push of a button, and Cristiano Ronaldo became a partner with his own collections.

Jacob & Co. remains privately owned by Jacob Arabo and his family, with its jewellery business headquartered in New York and its high-watchmaking arm based in Geneva, positioning itself at the extreme, theatrical end of luxury watchmaking.

name: Harry Winston
tagline: The 'King of Diamonds' whose Opus series reinvented independent watchmaking
summary: Harry Winston is a New York high-jewellery house founded in 1932, famous for historic diamonds such as the Hope Diamond. Its watch division, based in Geneva and owned with the whole house by the Swatch Group since 2013, blends gem-setting with complications, and its Opus series gave a platform to leading independent watchmakers.
history:
Harry Winston, the son of a small New York jeweller, founded Harry Winston Inc. in 1932 and built his reputation by buying historic jewellery collections and famous stones, recutting and resetting them. Over his career he handled many of the world's great diamonds, including the Jonker, the Vargas and the Hope Diamond, which he donated to the Smithsonian Institution in 1958 by sending it through the US mail. He became known as the 'King of Diamonds' and the 'jeweller to the stars', lending jewels to Hollywood actresses for the Academy Awards.

After his death in 1978, his son Ronald Winston led the company and in 1989 launched its first watch collection, the Premier, a ladies' watch that combined fine jewellery with Swiss movements. A dedicated watch company was established in Geneva, and the house expanded into men's watches with the Ocean and Midnight collections.

In 2001 Maximilian Büsser, then head of the watch division, created the Opus series, inviting an independent watchmaker to create an annual limited-edition piece under both names. Opus 1 was made with François-Paul Journe, and later editions involved Vianney Halter, Felix Baumgartner of Urwerk, Andreas Strehler and others. The series helped bring independent watchmaking into the mainstream. The Histoire de Tourbillon series followed with multi-axis tourbillons.

In 2013 the Swatch Group bought Harry Winston's jewellery and watch business from the Canadian mining company then known as Harry Winston Diamond Corporation. Today the house's Geneva workshops produce the Premier, Midnight, Ocean and Emerald lines alongside high-complication and métiers d'art pieces.

name: Corum
tagline: La Chaux-de-Fonds creatives behind the Golden Bridge, Admiral and Coin Watch
summary: Corum was founded in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1955 and became known for daring designs: the nautical-flagged Admiral, the Coin Watch made from a gold coin and the Golden Bridge baguette movement. After more than a decade under Hong Kong's Citychamp group, it returned to Swiss ownership through a management buyout in 2025.
history:
Corum was founded in 1955 in La Chaux-de-Fonds by Gaston Ries and his nephew René Bannwart, a watch designer who had worked at Omega and Patek Philippe. From the start the brand cultivated unconventional designs. The Admiral's Cup, launched in 1960, took its name from the famous sailing regatta and later adopted a twelve-sided case with nautical pennant flags in place of hour markers. In 1964 Corum introduced the Coin Watch, whose case and dial were made from a genuine US 20-dollar gold coin sliced in two, and it became a favourite of American presidents and celebrities.

Other imaginative pieces followed, including the Buckingham with an unusual case and the Romulus with Roman numerals engraved in the bezel. In 1980 Corum launched the Golden Bridge, designed by Vincent Calabrese, whose baguette movement is aligned in a single line and suspended between sapphire crystals, creating a striking linear look.

In 2000 Severin Wunderman, the former Gucci watch licensee, acquired Corum and injected new energy with pieces like the oversized Bubble. After his death in 2008, the brand was sold in 2013 to the Hong Kong-based China Haidian group, later renamed Citychamp Watch & Jewellery, which also owned Eterna. The following years were difficult amid declining sales and frequent management changes.

In 2025, the year of its 70th anniversary, Corum returned to 100% Swiss ownership through a management buyout led by Haso Mehmedovic, a former watchmaker and sales director who became CEO and chairman, backed by Swiss investors. The brand continues to focus on the Admiral, Golden Bridge, Bubble and heritage-inspired pieces.

name: Cartier
tagline: The jeweller of kings whose Santos and Tank defined the modern wristwatch
summary: Cartier, founded in Paris in 1847, is the world's second-largest Swiss-made watch brand by revenue and one of the most influential designers of wristwatch shapes. Owned by Richemont, it created the Santos in 1904 and the Tank in 1917, and today sells an estimated 700,000 watches a year.
history:
Louis-François Cartier took over the Paris jewellery workshop of his master, Adolphe Picard, in 1847. His son Alfred and grandsons Louis, Pierre and Jacques turned the firm into an international house with branches in Paris (13 rue de la Paix from 1899), London and New York, supplying royal courts across Europe and earning King Edward VII's description of Cartier as 'the jeweller of kings and the king of jewellers'.

Louis Cartier was the creative force behind the house's watches. In 1904 he designed a flat square wristwatch with exposed screws for his friend, the Brazilian aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont, who wanted to read the time without letting go of his controls. The Santos was sold commercially from 1911. The Tortue followed in 1912, and in 1917 Louis drew the Tank, inspired by the outline of Renault tanks on the Western Front, with the brancards forming the lugs. Cartier also patented a deployant buckle in 1910. Movements were supplied by partners such as Edmond Jaeger, and Cartier produced remarkable mystery clocks.

After the family generation passed, the firm was split and then reunited in the 1970s by an investor group led by Joseph Kanoui and backed by the Rupert family's Rembrandt Group. The affordable 'Les Must de Cartier' line of the 1970s broadened the audience, and the Crash, the Pasha and the Panthère became cult designs. Cartier became the cornerstone of the Vendôme group, later Richemont, formed in 1988.

Cartier opened its manufacture in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 2001 and developed in-house movements such as the 1904 MC. The Ballon Bleu (2007) became a bestseller, and relaunches of the Santos (2018), Tank Must (2021, including the solar-powered SolarBeat) and the Cartier Privé series fuelled a boom, making Cartier Morgan Stanley's number two Swiss watch brand by 2025.

name: Van Cleef & Arpels
tagline: Place Vendôme poetry: watches that tell time as stories
summary: Van Cleef & Arpels is a Paris high-jewellery maison founded in 1896 and owned by Richemont. Its Poetic Complications, such as the Lady Arpels Pont des Amoureux and Midnight Planétarium, use mechanical animations, enamel and gems to turn time-telling into narrative art.
history:
Van Cleef & Arpels grew out of a love story: in 1895 Alfred Van Cleef, son of a stone-cutter, married Estelle Arpels, daughter of a precious-stone dealer. The following year Alfred and Estelle's brother Charles Arpels founded the business, and in 1906 they opened a boutique at 22 Place Vendôme in Paris, where the maison remains today. Estelle's brothers Julien and Louis later joined the firm.

The house became famous for inventive jewellery. In 1933 it patented the Mystery Set, a technique in which gemstones are set without visible prongs. Around 1935 it created the Cadenas watch, a discreet bracelet watch shaped like a padlock that became a favourite of the Duchess of Windsor, and in the 1930s and 40s it produced jewellery watches and minaudières. The Alhambra four-leaf clover motif, launched in 1968, became its best-known jewellery design, and the house expanded to New York in 1939.

Family control gave way in 1999 when the Vendôme group, now Richemont, took a majority stake, completing its acquisition by 2003. Under chairman Nicolas Bos the maison developed a distinctive watchmaking identity, with workshops in Geneva. The Poetic Complications, starting with the Lady Arpels Pont des Amoureux in 2010, use retrograde and animated mechanisms to tell stories: two lovers meeting on a Paris bridge, planets orbiting the sun in the Midnight Planétarium of 2014, and flowers opening in the Lady Arpels Heures Florales.

Today Van Cleef & Arpels is one of Richemont's most profitable jewellery maisons, and its watches, many produced in small series with enamel and gem-setting, are regularly awarded at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève.

name: Bulgari
tagline: Roman jeweller turned ultra-thin record-breaker with the Octo Finissimo
summary: Bulgari (styled Bvlgari) is a Roman jeweller founded in 1884 and owned by LVMH since 2011. Its watchmaking arm in Neuchâtel and Le Sentier has set multiple ultra-thin world records with the Octo Finissimo, while the Serpenti and Bulgari Bulgari remain design icons.
history:
Sotirios Voulgaris, a Greek silversmith from Epirus, emigrated to Italy and opened his first shop in Rome in 1884. The flagship on Via dei Condotti opened in 1905, and under his sons Giorgio and Costantino the house moved from silver to bold, colourful high jewellery that, by the 1950s and 60s, adorned film stars such as Elizabeth Taylor during the 'Hollywood on the Tiber' era. The Latinised 'Bvlgari' logo, inspired by classical Roman inscriptions, became its signature.

Bulgari's first Serpenti bracelet watches appeared in the late 1940s, with coiled snake bodies made of flexible Tubogas gold. In 1977 the Bulgari Bulgari watch, with the brand name engraved twice on the bezel like an ancient Roman coin, became a global success, and in 1982 the company founded Bulgari Time in Neuchâtel to develop its watchmaking.

The brand went public in 1995 and in 2000 bought the Daniel Roth and Gérald Genta watch companies, gaining movement expertise and the rights to Genta designs. The Octo, launched in 2012 from a Genta-era case concept combining an octagon with a round bezel, became the platform for Bulgari's technical ambitions. In 2011 LVMH acquired the company.

From 2014 the Octo Finissimo series set a string of world records for thinness, including the thinnest tourbillon, minute repeater, automatic watch and chronograph, and the Octo Finissimo Ultra of 2022 measured just 1.80 mm. A later chronometer-certified Octo Finissimo Ultra COSC reclaimed the record at 1.70 mm. Serpenti remains central to its women's watches, and the Octo Finissimo has since been extended with a smaller 37 mm size.

name: Hermès
tagline: The Paris saddler whose watches play with time, leather and wit
summary: Hermès, the family-controlled Paris luxury house founded in 1837, makes watches through La Montre Hermès in Biel, established in 1978. It holds stakes in movement, case and dial makers, and its Arceau, Cape Cod, Slim d'Hermès and H08 collections blend equestrian heritage with playful complications.
history:
Thierry Hermès opened a harness workshop in Paris in 1837, making fine saddlery for the carriage trade. His son Charles-Émile moved the business to 24 rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré in 1880, and as cars replaced horses, grandson Émile-Maurice Hermès diversified into leather goods, luggage and accessories. In 1912 the house made a leather strap with a pocket to hold a watch on the wrist, and it sold watches from partners such as Universal and Jaeger-LeCoultre in its Paris store.

Hermès established its own watch subsidiary, La Montre Hermès, in Biel/Bienne in 1978. That same year designer Henri d'Origny created the Arceau, with its round case and stirrup-shaped asymmetric lugs and slanting numerals that seem to gallop. D'Origny also designed the Cape Cod in 1991, a square within a rectangle inspired by the chaîne d'ancre link, later worn on the long double-tour strap created with Martin Margiela.

In the 2000s the house pursued vertical integration, acquiring a 25% stake in Vaucher Manufacture Fleurier in 2006, and later the case maker Joseph Erard and dial maker Natéber. This enabled the Slim d'Hermès of 2015, with numerals drawn by typographer Philippe Apeloig, and a series of 'poetic' complications such as the Arceau Le Temps Suspendu of 2011, whose hands can be made to stop time at the push of a button.

The cushion-shaped H08 sports watch followed in 2021, and Hermès has won prizes at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève for its métiers d'art dials. The house remains majority-controlled by descendants of Thierry Hermès.

name: Chanel
tagline: Couture house turned serious watchmaker: the ceramic J12 and in-house calibres
summary: Chanel, the fashion house founded by Gabrielle 'Coco' Chanel in 1910, entered watchmaking in 1987 with the Première and revolutionised the market in 2000 with the high-tech ceramic J12. Privately owned by the Wertheimer family, it now produces in-house movements in La Chaux-de-Fonds and holds stakes in several independent watchmakers.
history:
Gabrielle 'Coco' Chanel opened a millinery shop at 21 rue Cambon in Paris in 1910 and went on to transform women's fashion with jersey dresses, the little black dress, Chanel No. 5 perfume and the tweed suit. Since the 1950s the company has been owned by the Wertheimer family, originally Chanel's business partners in perfume, and it remains privately held under Alain and Gérard Wertheimer.

Chanel's watchmaking began in 1987 with the Première, a women's watch whose octagonal case recalled the stopper of the No. 5 bottle and the shape of Place Vendôme, worn on a chain bracelet interlaced with leather. In 1993 the house acquired the Swiss case maker G&F Châtelain in La Chaux-de-Fonds, which became its watch manufacture. The real turning point came in 2000 with the J12, designed by artistic director Jacques Helleu and inspired by America's Cup racing yachts. Made of scratch-resistant high-tech black ceramic, followed by white in 2003, it became one of the defining watches of the decade.

Chanel then pursued watchmaking credibility. It took stakes in independent makers such as Romain Gauthier and, in 2018, F.P. Journe, and in 2019 bought into movement maker Kenissi, which supplies Tudor. The Monsieur de Chanel of 2016, its first men's watch with an in-house jumping-hour and retrograde-minute calibre, was followed by the Boy·Friend skeleton and the J12's 2019 redesign with the Kenissi-made Calibre 12.1.

Today Chanel's watch collections include the J12, Première, Boy·Friend, Code Coco and Monsieur, alongside high-jewellery watches, while the company's global headquarters are in London.

name: Louis Vuitton
tagline: The trunk maker's Geneva watchmaking, reborn with the 2023 Tambour
summary: Louis Vuitton, the Paris trunk maker founded in 1854 and the flagship of LVMH, has made watches since the 2002 Tambour. With its own La Fabrique du Temps manufacture in Geneva, it moved decisively upmarket with the redesigned integrated-bracelet Tambour of 2023 and collaborations with leading independent watchmakers.
history:
Louis Vuitton, a carpenter's son from the Jura, walked to Paris as a teenager and trained as a box-maker and packer. In 1854 he opened his own workshop, and his flat-topped, stackable trunks, the Damier canvas of 1888 and the Monogram canvas of 1896 created by his son Georges made the house synonymous with luxury travel. In 1987 it merged with Moët Hennessy to form LVMH, of which it is the largest brand.

Louis Vuitton entered watchmaking in 2002 with the Tambour, whose drum-shaped case with the brand's name engraved around the side became its signature. In 2011 the company acquired La Fabrique du Temps, a Geneva complications workshop, and later built a manufacture in Meyrin, adding case- and dial-making capability. Its high-end pieces included the Escale Worldtime of 2014 and the Tambour Moon series, and in 2017 the Tambour Horizon became its connected smartwatch.

In 2021 Jean Arnault, son of LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, took charge of the watch division and repositioned it firmly in serious watchmaking. The completely redesigned Tambour of 2023, with a slim integrated steel bracelet and the in-house LFT023 micro-rotor calibre, was well received by collectors. Louis Vuitton also launched the Louis Vuitton Watch Prize for Independent Creatives and partnered with independents, notably with Rexhep Rexhepi of Akrivia on the LVRR-01 chiming chronograph in 2024. It also relaunched the Escale and introduced the Tambour Taiko.

The maison's watches are made in Geneva, while its headquarters remain in Paris.
